stops.name: Mainz, the ransom paid, the release
stops.campa: Eleanor herself, not trusting the business to any deputy, crosses to Germany with the ransom in the depths of winter to see her favorite son delivered with her own eyes. At Mainz on the fourth of February the sum is paid, the hostages exchanged, and Richard — in a final humiliation the Emperor extracts at the last hour — is made to kneel and surrender England itself as a fief held from the Empire, receiving it back at once as vassal, a homage the English council will simply refuse to honor afterward. Then, at last, mother and son ride west together, free, toward the sea and home.

stops.name: Sandwich, the landing
stops.campa: Richard lands at Sandwich in Kent on the thirteenth of March, more than four years after he first sailed for the Holy Land, king of a country he has now spent barely six months of his reign actually inhabiting. Church bells ring the length of the Kentish coast; he goes first, on foot, to give thanks at the shrine of Thomas Becket in Canterbury before anything else — the murdered archbishop his father's great sin, the pilgrimage a son's atonement offered on his own behalf as much as his father's. Then he turns toward London, toward the throne, and toward a brother who thought him dead or fixed for good in a German cell.

stops.name: Winchester, the second coronation
stops.campa: To wash out the stain of captivity — a king who has knelt to an emperor must be seen, publicly, wearing his crown as a free man again — Richard holds a second, ceremonial crown-wearing at Winchester Cathedral on the seventeenth of April, the old West Saxon capital, robed and crowned anew before the assembled magnates of England. It is not a fresh coronation in the sacramental sense, no new anointing, but theater as carefully staged as any of his sieges: the message, to England and to Philip of France alike, is that the Lionheart is home, unbroken, and already turning to the war he has been cheated of for five years running.

stops.name: Fréteval, the rout of the French king
stops.campa: Within weeks Richard is in Normandy making war on Philip Augustus, who spent the captivity years carving into Angevin lands on the promise Richard would never return. At Fréteval, near Vendôme, Richard catches the French army in retreat and routs it outright; Philip flees the field so fast he abandons his entire baggage train, including his personal seal and the royal archives — charters, tax rolls, the names of every spy and agent Philip keeps inside Richard's own duchies. It is as much an intelligence coup as a battle, and hands Richard, for the first time since the crusade, the clear upper hand over the king who once called himself his brother-in-arms.

stops.name: Les Andelys, Château Gaillard, the year-old daughter
stops.campa: On a chalk spur above the Seine at Les Andelys, in defiance of a treaty forbidding him to fortify the spot, Richard raises in a single year the castle he calls his masterpiece: triple-walled, machicolated, its keep faced with pointed buttresses no siege engine of the age can find purchase against. Riding out to see it nearing completion, he is said to look up at the pale new stone and call it, in delight, how fair is this year-old daughter of mine — Château Gaillard, the saucy, the insolent castle. He boasts he could hold it were its walls made of butter. Philip Augustus will take it after Richard's death, but never in his lifetime.
stops.quote: Behold, how fair is this year-old daughter of mine!
stops.quote_source: Richard on Château Gaillard, c. 1197-98 — the saying is carried by the Anglo-Norman chronicle tradition; the wording here is the received English rendering, and no single chronicle text could be fixed as its origin

stops.name: Châlus-Chabrol, the crossbow bolt and the forgiveness
stops.campa: Besieging the minor castle of Châlus-Chabrol over a disputed treasure of Roman gold, which Richard claims by his overlord's right, he rides too close to the walls unarmored in the evening light, and a crossbow bolt fired by a defender, a boy some chroniclers name Bertrand de Gourdon, strikes him in the shoulder. A clumsy surgeon's cutting turns the wound gangrenous within days. Brought the boy who shot him, and told he had lost a father and two brothers to Richard's wars, the dying king forgives him outright: live on, he says, and by my bounty see the light of day.
stops.quote: Live on, and by my bounty behold the light of day.
stops.quote_source: attributed last mercy of Richard I to his killer, Châlus-Chabrol, March 1199 (tradition, Roger of Howden)

stops.name: Fontevraud and Rouen, the burial divided
stops.campa: Richard dies on the sixth of April in his mother's arms; Mercadier, his mercenary captain, flays the boy who killed him alive despite the pardon, a mercy his own men refuse to honor. His body, by his own instruction, is divided in the old royal fashion: heart embalmed and sent to Rouen, to lie in its own small tomb in the cathedral; entrails left near Châlus, by one tradition at the abbey of Charroux; the rest carried to Fontevraud in Anjou and laid beside the father he fought nearly all his life, under an effigy holding a crown he wore, in the end, for barely six months at home.
